 G) SCHEDULE CONTROL

SCHEDULE CONTROL
Paragon’s Project Team understands the importance of keeping a project on schedule. We have prepared a project schedule
to illustrate the representative tasks necessary complete this project. Each milestone and delivery date has been evaluated
in detail to ensure a realistic approach and provide right-of-way prior to the City’s construction date. Right-of-way tasks
are often on the critical path of schedules. Therefore, we prioritize high risk matters and itemize any action items into
smaller tasks. In the event of schedule slippage, Paragon’s Project Manager will create workable solutions with the City
to accelerate the schedule, such as providing additional staff or working additional hours. Where appropriate, we also
rearrange project tasks to be completed in parallel instead of in sequence. By doing this, we can accelerate work on current
tasks to get back on track for future tasks. In addition, we can identify future tasks that can be started earlier to make up
for time.

PREVIOUS EXPERIENCE

Paragon has successfully completed numerous sewer easement projects, including the Durfee Avenue Grade Separation
in the City of Pico Rivera, for the Alameda Corridor-East Construction Authority. The project required an innovative
approach to mitigating the impact of constructing critical components of the grade separation, specifically, a series of
sewer lines. For nearly 25 years, in the City of Pico Rivera, Fiesta Hall has been a landmark business serving Pico Rivera
and adjacent communities. Located at 4754 Durfee Avenue, the property was originally identified as a full-take acquisition
and relocation in order to allow for the necessary construction of several sewer lines and other above and below ground
utilities. After various meetings with the property/business owners, it became clear to the project team that the business
owners strongly opposed relocating their business. By assembling the key project stakeholders - the client, the project
engineering firm, the City of Pico Rivera, and the owners of Fiesta Hall - Paragon prompted a collaborative effort to
redesign the entry/access to the banquet hall property, a re-route of the sewer line easements, electrical lines, and water
lines, and a modification of the on-site parking and circulation. The result was an improved overall project design with
efforts redirected toward partial acquisitions in lieu of a full acquisition, which allowed Fiesta Hall to continue to serve the
community and keep their staff fully employed. The result of this shift in plan direction achieved a $1.5 million savings in
acquisition and relocation cost for the client and minimized the impact to the property owner and the community.

  FROM THE DATE OF THE NOTICE TO PROCEED

RECOMMENDATION

Staff recommend that the City Council:

  1. Approve Construction Agreement No. A-9799 with Vance Corporation for PN
  917A, Avenue R from 25th Street East to Tackstem Avenue (Project), for a total
  not to exceed amount of $12,777,832, which includes a contract amount of
  $11,616,210, plus a 10% contingency amount of $1,161,622 for a term of 120
  working days from the date of the Notice to Proceed;

  2. Authorize the City Manager or his designee to execute Agreement No. A-9799
  with Vance Corporation, including minimal and/or non-substantial changes; and,

  3. Authorize the City Manager or his designee to approve change orders for
  additional or changed scopes of work up to the 10% contingency amount
  approved by the Council.

BACKGROUND

As part of the Citywide Annual Pavement Maintenance Program, this Project prioritizes
roadway resurfacing to boost structural integrity and pedestrian/motorist safety. The
segment along with Avenue R was selected based on the last available Pavement
Management Program for having a PCI lower than 50 and a continuation of the recently
completed Avenue R Complete Street Project. The project is to address the deficiencies
and provide a smoother, safer ride to the motorists, and enhance safety for pedestrians
and cyclists.
 Report to Mayor and City Council
Re: Approve Agreement with Vance Construction for PN 917A
June 2, 2026
Page 2

The Project scope includes full-depth reclamation, pulverizing 18 inches of existing
asphalt and underlying base, followed by pavement replacement (base and surface
courses). Additional work includes reconstructing curb ramps to meet ADA
requirements, replacing traffic signal detectors, installing high-visibility crosswalks,
modifying bicycle video detection, and installing new pavement markings/signage.

Local paving companies were contacted during the bidding process to raise awareness
among local businesses in bidding on the job.

Construction is anticipated to take approximately one hundred twenty (120) working
days from the date the City issues the Notice to Proceed.

Public Outreach

The selected Construction Management Team, Z&K Consultants, will take the lead and
implement all public outreach efforts to ensure communications are accurate, timely,
and aligned with project phasing and traffic control activities. Public outreach will include,
but not be limited to, mailers, virtual meetings, and website or social media updates. All
notifications distributed will be bilingual.

Outreach efforts will be coordinated with construction activities to ensure that residents,
businesses, and schools receive advance notice of construction schedules, lane
closures, and access impacts. Special attention will be given to coordination with nearby
schools to avoid peak drop-off and pick-up periods and ensure safe pedestrian access.

DISCUSSION

The Project was advertised for construction bids via the PlanetBids electronic platform
on March 18, 2026. Six (6) bids were received on April 20, 2026, and are listed below:

Bidder  Location  Amount
1. Vance Corporation  Beaumont, CA  $11,616,210.62
2. Hardy & Harper  Lake Forest, CA  $12,650,000.00
3. Calmex Engineering Inc.  Bloomington, CA  $12,713,435.67
4. C.A. Rasmussen, Inc.  Valencia, CA  $13,527,002.58
5. Sully-Miller Contracting Co.  Brea, CA  $13,697,891.73
6. Security Paving Company, Inc.  Westlake Village, CA  $13,887,320.30

The item was scheduled to go before the Council on May 5, 2026. On that day, the City
Clerk received a letter of protest from the second-low bidder alleging unfair business
practices and collusion. Out of an abundance of caution, Public Works staff decided to
 Report to Mayor and City Council
Re: Approve Agreement with Vance Construction for PN 917A
June 2, 2026
Page 3

defer the award until a thorough review could be conducted to fully investigate the
alleged impropriety. After a comprehensive review by staff and the City Attorney’s office,
there is no evidence that there is an unfair advantage to the low bidder. Every potential
bidder had equal access to the civil designer and the Plans, Specifications, and
Addenda. The City found no evidence of collusion, bid rigging, or improper coordination
between Vance Corporation and any City consultant or employee. The protest was
rejected.

Based on the bid analysis, Vance Corporation submitted the lowest responsive bid and
secured the required 10% bid bond. References have been checked, and staff
recommend that the City Council award Project No. 917A to Vance Corporation in the
amount of $11,616,210, with a 10% contingency.

Vance Corporation has completed successful projects for agencies such as the City of
Cathedral City, County of Riverside, and City of Chino Hills.

2021-044. The primary goal of the Palmdale EIFD is to implement the Palmdale
Enhanced Infrastructure Financing Plan to attract new private sector investment,
accelerate development in key areas of the City, stimulate job creation, expand housing
opportunities, and strengthen local and regional transportation options for the region.

members of the City Council, a public member selected by the Council, one County
member, and a public member selected by the County.

Highway, Suite B, Palmdale, CA.

resignation, this action allows the City Council to nominate and appoint one public

BACKGROUND

On May 12, 2022, the Planning Commission adopted Resolution No. PC-2022-020
approving Minor Site Plan Review (MSPR) 22-002 for the development of the 48-unit
affordable housing project and recommending City Council approval of a form of AGR
22-002 for the associated Density Bonus Agreement. On May 17, 2022, the Director of
Economic and Community Development approved MSPR 22-002, which established an
expiration date of May 18, 2023. On May 18, 2022, the City Council adopted Resolution
No. CC 2022-059, approving a form of Agreement (AGR) 22-002 (A-7912). On May 18,
2023, MSPR 22-002 expired, requiring submittal of a new application. Subsequently,
the Director of Economic and Community Development approved MSPR 25-0005 on
September 17, 2025, which established an expiration date of September 17, 2028. On
March 30, 2026, an application was filed with the City to amend the previously approved
Agreement (AGR) 22-002 (A-7912).

DISCUSSION

The application proposes to amend the Density Bonus Agreement to add one concession,
as set forth in Exhibit E of Resolution No. CC 2026-028 for the approved affordable
housing project pursuant to Density Bonus Law (Government Code Section 65915) and
Palmdale Municipal Code (PMC) Section 17.25.020.I.

The approved project includes 48 dwelling units with 100 percent of the units designated
for households with incomes not exceeding the low-income threshold established by the
California Department of Housing and Community Development (HCD). In accordance
with the State Density Bonus Law, the applicant can request an unlimited number of
waivers of development standards that would preclude the development and a maximum
of three concessions from the City’s development standards to facilitate the provision of
affordable housing.

A density bonus is a request to increase the overall number of housing units that a
developer may build on a site in exchange for providing affordable housing. State Density
Bonus Law, pursuant to Section 65915 et seq of the California Government Code, offers
incentives that are intended to encourage the development of affordable housing.

A Minor Site Plan Review and Density Bonus Agreement were required to allow the
proposed development. The project was reviewed for consistency with applicable design
standards and policies related to density, site planning, circulation, landscaping, and
building form and related standards. At the time of approval, the applicant did not request
incentives or concessions, but did request the use of the density bonus parking ratio.

The proposed amendment to the previously approved Density Bonus Agreement includes
a request for one concession as follows:

  A concession to the Palmdale Transit Area Specific Plan (PTASP) Figure 5.4.
  (Development Standards Table), which requires residential ground-floor heights of
  at least 18 feet and typical upper-floor heights of at least 10 feet in the Urban
  Center (T5) zone. Instead, the ground-floor height will be 12 feet, and the upper-
  floor heights will be 9.5 feet.

The requested concession reduces development costs by eliminating the need for
manlifts during construction, which would be required if the building height exceeds 60
feet, and would cost approximately $1.7 million. The additional cost would create a
hardship for the project and would make the affordable housing project infeasible.

This requested concession is intended to facilitate the construction of high-quality,
affordable housing while accommodating the construction costs and design needs. The
project complies with all other applicable zoning regulations and supports the City’s goals
for housing production and affordability.

Staff has determined that granting the additional concession listed above will result in
actual and identifiable cost reductions to provide affordable housing. In addition, the
proposed project will help meet the City’s Regional Housing Needs Assessment (RHNA)
allocation.

and/or its assigns (“Owner”), as follows:

  RECITALS

  A.  Owner is the owner of a fee interest in certain real property located in the
City of Palmdale, County of Los Angeles, State of California, identified as APN 3008-040-
012, located at 38732 9th Street E., Palmdale, CA and legally described in Exhibit “A”
attached hereto and incorporated by reference (“Property”).

  B.  Owner will construct a 48-unit affordable housing development, with three
residential buildings, included amenities, and retail units (collectively, the “Residential
Development”). The Residential Development provides for units of varying types, two-
and three-bedroom flats. The Residential Development will provide 50 parking stalls
onsite.

  C.  The residential portion of the Residential Development will consist of 48
residential units for very low-income and low-income individuals and families. One
hundred percent (100%) of the units, with the exception of the manager’s unit, will be
available to and occupied by households whose incomes do not exceed the maximum
income of low income households in Los Angeles County as determined by the California
Department of Housing and Community Development.

  D.  Under Government Code Section 65915, et seq. and Palmdale Municipal
Code, Section 17.25.110, the City must, upon the request of an applicant, grant a density
bonus and/or certain incentives/concessions or waivers/modifications for any
development applicant that seeks and agrees to construct a minimum number of housing
units that are affordable to low or very low-income households (“Density Bonus Law”).

  E.  The subject site has a General Plan Land Use Designation of SP (Palmdale
Transit Area Specific Plan) and T-5 (Urban Center) zone, with a density of 30-50 dwelling
units per acre. The Property is 1.02 acres allowing 48 units to be developed on the
Property. The Residential Development does not require a density bonus. Density
Bonus Law requires that because 100% of the resident units in the Residential
Development will be affordable to “lower-income households” per section 50079.5 of
the California Health and Safety Code, Government Code section 65915(d)(2)(D)
entitles the Residential Development to four incentives or concessions. Density Bonus
Law requires the City to grant to the Residential Development parking ratios that do not
exceed 1 space per studio or one-bedroom unit, 1.5 spaces per two-bedroom or three-
bedroom unit, or 2.5 spaces per four-bedroom unit. Therefore, Density Bonus Law
requires the City to permit the Residential Development’s proposed parking ratio of 1.5
spaces per unit for the two- and three-bedroom flats.

  F.  The subject site has a General Plan Land Use Designation of SP (Palmdale
Transit Area Specific Plan) and T5 (Urban Center) zone, with a ground floor height of 18
feet and a typical upper floor at 10 feet. Density Bonus Law allows the City to provide a
concession to allow the Residential Development’s proposed ground level garage height
of 12 feet with a typical upper floor height of 9.5 feet.

  G.  City and Owner enter into this Agreement pursuant to and in accordance
with Government Code Section 65915, et seq., and Section 17.25.110 of the Palmdale
Municipal Code, in order to provide housing for lower-income households.

  H.  The City finds that permitting the parking ratio under Section E, above, will
result in actual and identifiable cost reductions to provide for affordable housing cost, will
not have an adverse impact upon public health and safety, the physical environment, or

RECOMMENDATION

Staff recommend that the City Council:

  A. Hold a public hearing to accept public testimony; and,

  B. Receive and file the Fiscal Year (FY) 2026-27 Annual Employee Vacancy Report,
  in accordance with Assembly Bill 2561.

BACKGROUND

On September 22, 2024, Governor Newsom signed Assembly Bill 2561 (AB 2561) into
law, which became effective on January 1, 2025. AB 2561 requires public agencies to
address the status of vacancies. The California Legislature recognized that vacancies
in the public sector pose challenges that can and negatively impact the delivery of public
services.

DISCUSSION

AB 2561 requires the City to present the status of vacancies, recruitment efforts, and
retention efforts at a public hearing held at least once each fiscal year prior to adoption of
the final budget. Specifically, the statute requires public agencies to:

    Report job vacancies, recruitment, and retention efforts;
    Identify policies or practices that may lead to obstacles or negatively impact the
  hiring process;
    Provide recognized bargaining units an opportunity to participate in the public
  hearing; and,
    If the number of job vacancies within a single bargaining unit meets or exceeds
  20% of the total number of authorized full-time positions in a particular bargaining
  unit, provide additional data upon request of the recognized employee
  organization, including the total number of job vacancies within a bargaining unit,

RECOMMENDATION

Staff recommend that the City Council:

  1. Hold a public hearing to accept public testimony;

  2. Approve Economic Development Subsidy Agreements; and,

  3. Authorize the City Manager or his designee to execute Agreements, including
  minimal and/or non-substantial changes.

BACKGROUND

The City continues to pursue economic development initiatives that support local
businesses, retain jobs, and generate additional revenue for the City. Local automobile
dealerships are a significant component of the City’s sales tax base and contribute to
the community’s economic vitality.

To evaluate potential strategies to support and retain the City’s automobile dealership
sector, the City Council established an ad-hoc committee consisting of two City
Councilmembers appointed by a majority of the City Council. The ad-hoc committee met
with staff and discussed the economic conditions affecting the local automotive retail
sector, as well as potential strategies to encourage continued investment and business
activity in the City. Following these discussions and the review of available options, the
ad hoc committee directed staff to draft an economic subsidy agreement with
participating automobile dealerships to support local business activity and maintain a
strong sales tax base. At the May 5, 2026, City Council meeting, the City Council voted
to direct staff to bring forward the draft agreement for discussion and consideration at
the June 2, 2026, meeting.

The attached Economic Development Subsidy Agreement has been developed and is
now being presented to the City Council for discussion and consideration.

Statement of Public Purpose

The City Council finds that the economic development subsidy serves the following
public purposes:

    Supporting the retention and stability of existing local businesses;
    Promoting continued private investment within the City;
    Maintaining and enhancing the City’s sales tax base;
    Supporting employment opportunities for residents; and
    Strengthening the overall economic vitality of the community.

The subsidy is intended to produce long-term fiscal and economic benefits that outweigh
the initial public investment.

Projected Tax Revenue

Based on current estimates, the participating dealerships are expected to generate
approximately:

    Annual Sales Tax Revenue: $2,750,000
    Total Projected Revenue Over Term: $20,175,000

These projections are based on historical sales data, anticipated business activity, and
reasonable economic assumptions. Actual revenues may vary due to market conditions
and other factors outside the City’s control.

Employment Impact

While Government Code Section 53083 requires disclosure of the estimated number of
jobs created, the primary purpose of the proposed economic development subsidy is
the retention of existing jobs within the City’s automobile dealership sector. The
participating dealerships currently provide a significant number of local employment
opportunities, and the subsidy is intended to support ongoing operations, maintain
competitiveness, and prevent potential job loss due to market conditions and regional
competition.

The proposed loan is primarily intended to support ongoing business operations and
retention of existing employment opportunities. The applicant(s) did not provide an
estimate of new jobs anticipated to be created.

BACKGROUND

Each year the City is required to adopt a budget for its operation. The budget serves as
the City’s financial plan for the Fiscal Year beginning July 1 through June 30. It defines
City priorities for the provision of services to the community.

According to the Palmdale Municipal Code: Chapter 3.04 Budget Adoption Procedures,
the City Manager shall submit a proposed budget to the City Council no later than May
31 of each year. The proposed budget was brought before the City Council on May 5,
2026. Additionally, the City Council shall conduct a public hearing on the proposed budget
before adoption and shall adopt a budget prescribing the spending policy of the City for
the ensuing fiscal year on or before the thirtieth day of June of each year.

consideration.

Fund, Special Revenue, Enterprise, Debt Service, and Capital Funds.

Revenues
Estimating revenues for the upcoming fiscal year and forecasting out-years is essential
to the budget development process. Revenue projections are formed by analyzing prior-
year actual receipts, trends, new revenue sources, grant opportunities, service fees, and
the State economic outlook. Citywide revenues are estimated to be $471,313,960.

The General Fund is the City’s primary source of unrestricted revenue, with projected
resources totaling $128,080,100. These resources are comprised of property tax, sales
tax, other local taxes, fees, and charges for services. In November 2024, voters approved
Measure PD, which increased the local sales tax rate by ¾ cent. This measure is
expected to generate approximately $23.8 million in Fiscal Year 2026-27 and is included
in the General Fund. Additionally, Measure AV, a general sales tax, is projected to
generate $23.8 million in Fiscal Year 2026-27. While not required, the City reports
Measure AV revenue separately from the General Fund to ensure transparency and
accountability to the Measure AV Oversight Committee.

Operating Appropriations
The proposed FY 2026-27 operating budget includes $403,521,790 across all City funds.
Of this total, $127,182,550 represents the General Fund operating budget. The proposed
budget reflects a balanced and strategic approach to funding City operations and capital
projects. It maintains core service levels while addressing key areas such as public safety,
infrastructure, maintenance, and community programs. The proposed level of funding
ensures the City can continue delivering high-quality services to residents while
advancing long-term goals. The supporting schedules provide additional details on
appropriations.

Capital Improvement Program
The proposed Capital Improvement Budget totals $305,760,110 and includes previously
approved appropriations of $233,082,080 along with proposed additions of $72,678,030.
As capital projects often span multiple years, budgeted amounts may not be fully
expended within a single fiscal year. The attached schedules detail all previously
approved and proposed capital improvement projects.

  Bodies for the Fiscal Year 2026-27 for review, consideration and adoption; and,

  amended, on June 2, 2026, with public notice of the hearing published at least
  fourteen (14) days prior to said hearing, has further considered the proposed

  each entity, its citizens and businesspersons, to adopt the financial plan within the
  budget for the receipt and expenditure of public monies in Fiscal Year 2026-27;

  of operating expenditures, and that this Reserve Policy may fall below 20% in an

Terms
Accrual Basis – The method of accounting under which revenues and expenses are recorded when they occur,
regardless of the timing of related cash flows. Expenses are recorded at the time liabilities are incurred and
revenues are recorded when earned.
ACFR – The Annual Comprehensive Financial Report of the City which shows the financial status of the City.
Adoption – Formal action by the City Council that sets the spending limits for the fiscal year.
Appropriation – City Council authorization permitting the City to incur obligations and expend resources during
the fiscal year.

  Page 36 of 39
 Assessed Valuation – An official governmental value placed upon real estate or other property as a basis for
levying taxes.
Assessments – Levies that pay for improvements directly benefiting the property owners.
Audit – A review of the City’s accounts by an independent auditing firm to substantiate year-end fund balances,
reserves, and cash on hand.
Balanced Budget – The City’s operating revenues equal or exceed its operating expenditures.
Base Budget – Ongoing expense for personnel, contractual services, and the replacement of supplies and
equipment to maintain service levels previously authorized by the City Council.
Beginning / Ending Fund Balance – Unencumbered resources available in a fund from the prior/current year
after payment of the prior/current year’s expenses. This is not necessarily cash on hand.
Bond – A funding tool representing a written promise to pay a specific sum (face value or principal amount) in
the future (maturity date), plus interest. In local California government, bonds are only used to finance capital
improvements. There are two types of bonds:
General Obligation Bond – A bond requiring a 2/3 vote of the registered voters and backed by the full faith,
credit, and taxing power of the municipality.
Revenue Bond – A bond backed by either the revenue produced by the capital improvement or by commitment
of a specific revenue source.
Bond Proceeds – Debt issuances derived from the sale of bonds for the purpose of constructing major capital
facilities.
Budget – A financial plan listing proposed operational expenditures and revenue estimates for a particular time
period. The budget is proposed until it has been approved and adopted by the City Council. Palmdale’s budget
encompasses one fiscal year (July 1 to June 30).
Budget Message – A general discussion of the proposed budget as presented in writing by the City Manager to
the City Council. The message contains an explanation of principal budget items relative to the current year
adopted budget.
Capital Budget – The appropriation of bonds, operating revenue, or fees for improvements to City facilities
including buildings, streets, sewer lines, parks, traffic signals, drainage, etc.
Capital Improvement Program – A financial plan of proposed capital improvement projects with single and
multiple-year capital expenditures. The City of Palmdale's Capital Improvement Program is a ten-year plan,
which is updated annually.
Capital Improvement Projects (CIP) – A permanent addition to the City's assets, including the design, major
renovation, construction, or purchase of land, buildings, or facilities. This includes physical structural
improvements with a cost of $10,000 or more and a useful life of one year or more. Examples include a new
park, building modifications, traffic signals, resurfacing of streets and drainage improvements.
Capital Outlay – A budget category that budgets all equipment having a unit cost of more than $5,000. Capital
Outlay is budgeted in the operating budget as opposed to the capital improvement budget.
Contingency Fund – A budgetary reserve set aside for emergency or unanticipated expenditures.
Continuing Appropriation – Resources appropriated for a specific expenditure that is carried over from the prior
fiscal year.
Debt Ratio – Total debt divided by total assets. Used by Finance to assess fiscal health, internal controls, etc.
Debt Service – Payments of principal and interest on an obligation resulting from the issuance of bonds, notes,
or loans.
Debt Service Requirements – The amount of money required to pay principal and interest on outstanding debt
or to accumulate monies for future retirement of term bonds.

  Page 37 of 39
 Deficit – An excess of expenditures or expenses over resources.
Department – An organizational unit comprised of divisions or programs. This basic organizational unit of
government is functionally unique in its delivery of services.
Division – An organizational component of a department.
Encumbrances – Resources committed for future expenditures as a result of signing executory contracts such
as purchase orders and specific contracts for goods and services.
Enterprise Fund – An accounting entity that is financed and operated in a manner similar to private business
enterprises where the intent of the governing body is that the costs of providing goods and services to the
general public on a continuing basis is financed or recovered primarily through user charges.
Expenditure – The actual spending of funds set aside by an appropriation.
Fiscal Year – A 12-month accounting period used by the City. The City of Palmdale’s fiscal year begins July 1
and ends June 30.
Full Time Equivalent Position (FTE) – A part-time position converted to the decimal equivalent of a full-time
position based on 2,080 hours per year. For example, a part time typist working 20 hours per week would be
equivalent to 0.5 of a full-time position.
Fund – An independent fiscal and accounting entity with a self-balancing set of accounts to record revenue and
expenditures.
Fund Balance – The amount of financial resources available for use.
GAAP – Generally Accepted Accounting Principles. Uniform standards for financial accounting and recording,
encompassing the conventions, rules and procedures that define accepted accounting principles.
GASB – Governmental Accounting Standards Board is the current standards setting board for governmental
GAAP.
General Fund – The primary fund of the City used to account for all revenues and expenditures related to
municipal services and maintenance. Examples of departments financed by the General Fund include the City
Council, Finance, Planning and Law Enforcement.
General Obligation Bond – A bond requiring a 2/3 vote of the registered voters and backed by the full faith,
credit and taxing power of the municipality. This type of bond is used to finance capital improvements in local
California governments.
Goal – A statement of broad direction, purpose or intent based on the needs of the community. A goal is
general and timeless; that is, it is not concerned with a specific achievement in a given time period.
Grant – A contribution by a government or other organization to support a specific purpose, activity, or facility.
Infrastructure – Facilities upon which the continuance and growth of a community depend such as roads,
sewers, public buildings, parks, etc.
Interfund Transfers – The reallocation of money from one fund to another. The receiving fund must spend the
transferred money in a way that complies with any restrictions placed on the money when it was originally
received by the donor fund.
Investment Policy – A written, Council adopted policy delineating permitted investments of the City’s idle cash.
The City of Palmdale Investment Policy is typically updated and reaffirmed annually.
Major Fund – Any fund whose revenues or
expenditures, excluding other financing sources and uses, constitute more than 10%
of the revenues or expenditures of the appropriated budget.
Modified Accrual Basis – The accrual basis of accounting adapted to the governmental fund type spending
measurement focus. Under it, revenues are recognized when they become both measurable and available to
finance expenditures of the current period. Expenditures are recognized when the related fund liability is
incurred.
  Page 38 of 39
 Municipal Code – A book that contains City Council approved ordinances currently in effect. The Code defines
City policy with respect to areas such as planning, business licensing, etc.
Objective – Desired output-oriented accomplishments that can be measured and achieved within a given time
frame. Achievement of the objective advances the activity and organization toward a corresponding goal.
Operating Budget – Annual appropriation of funds for ongoing program costs including salaries and benefits,
services and supplies, debt service, capital outlay, and capital improvements.
Operating Expenditures – Expenditures for materials, supplies, and services which are ordinarily consumed
within a fiscal year and which are not included in departmental inventories.
Ordinance – A formal legislative enactment by the City Council that has the full force and effect of law within
City boundaries unless preempted by a higher form of law. An ordinance has a higher legal standing than a
resolution.
Palmdale Community Choice Aggregation (CCA) – The Palmdale CCA was formed in April 2019 through
California Choice Energy Authority (CalChoice) via City Council resolution to purchase power on behalf of the
City’s residents.
Palmdale Community Foundation – A 501(c)(3) nonprofit organization organized under the California Nonprofit
Public Benefit Corporation Law for public purposes.
PERS – Public Employees Retirement System.
Personnel – A budget category used to account for employee compensation including wages, salaries and
fringe benefits such as health, life, and disability insurance, retirement, and car allowance/mileage.
Program – A group of related activities performed by one or more organizational units for the purpose of
accomplishing a function.
Property Tax – An ad valorem tax on real property based upon the value of the property.
Property Transfer Tax – A tax imposed whenever the ownership of real property changes.
Reimbursement – Payment of amount remitted on behalf of another party, department, or fund.
Reserve – An account used to indicate that a portion of a fund's balance is legally restricted for a specific
purpose and is, therefore, not available for general appropriation.
Resolution – A special order of the City Council having a lower legal standing than an ordinance.
Resources – Total amounts available for appropriation including estimated revenues, fund transfers, and
beginning fund balances.
Revenue Bonds – A bond usually issued to construct facilities that is backed by either the revenue produced
by the capital improvement or by commitment of a specific revenue source.
Revenues – Money received by the City from taxes, fees, permits, licenses, interest, etc. or from other
governments during the fiscal year.
Special Revenue Funds – A fund used to account for revenues that are restricted in use by the City, State, or
Federal Government.
Subventions – Intergovernmental revenues paid to the City by another government, such as the State.
Transfer – A transfer is a transaction whereby the fund receiving the revenue transfers money to the fund
expending the revenue. An example would be an operating transfer from a Special Revenue Fund to the
Capital Projects Fund for construction expenditures.
User Fees/Charges – Charges of a voluntary nature paid by the person receiving the service in exchange for
the fee.

SUBJECT:  DISCUSSION AND DIRECTION REGARDING PREPARATION OF
  RESOLUTIONS RELATED TO THE POTENTIAL REPEAL AND
  DEFERRED IMPLEMENTATION OF MEASURE PD

RECOMMENDATION

Staff recommend that the City Council discuss and provide direction to staff regarding a
motion to:
  1. Draft a resolution ordering that an ordinance to fully repeal Measure PD be
  submitted to the voters at the General Municipal Election on November 3, 2026;

  2. Draft a resolution to defer implementation and collection of the full amount of the
  Measure PD sales and use tax increase, with such deferral remaining in effect
  until certification of the November 3, 2026, election results; and,

  3. Return both resolutions to the City Council for consideration and action at the
  next regularly scheduled City Council meeting.

BACKGROUND

At its May 5, 2026, meeting, the City Council directed staff to place this item on the agenda
for discussion.

Measure PD, the “Palmdale Essential Services Protection Measure,” was approved by
Palmdale voters at the November 5, 2024, General Municipal Election. The measure
authorized an increase to the City’s transactions and use tax rate. Following certification
of the election results, the City Council adopted the required ordinance implementing the
voter‑approved tax.

Under California Elections Code Sections 9222 and 1415, a City Council may submit a
proposed ordinance to the voters, including an ordinance that would repeal a previously
adopted or voter‑approved measure. Any such repeal ordinance must be placed before
the voters at a regular municipal election or at a special election called for that purpose.
 Report to Mayor and City Council
Re: Discussion and Direction Regarding Measure PD
June 2, 2026
Page 2

The next regularly scheduled General Municipal Election for the City of Palmdale will
occur on November 3, 2026.

DISCUSSION

If directed, staff will prepare a resolution placing an ordinance on the November 3, 2026,
ballot that would fully repeal Measure PD. Adoption of such a resolution would constitute
the Council’s formal action ordering the submission of the repeal ordinance to the voters,
consistent with Elections Code requirements.

The motion also proposes that the City Council consider a resolution deferring
implementation and collection of the full Measure PD tax rate until after November 3,
2026, election results are certified. A deferral resolution would not repeal or amend
Measure PD; rather, it would direct staff to continue collecting the tax at the currently
implemented rate and to postpone any increase to the full authorized rate pending the
outcome of the 2026 election.

If the Council provides direction to proceed, staff will prepare both resolutions and place
them on the agenda for the next regularly scheduled City Council meeting for formal
consideration and possible action.
